# Patent law (`patents`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by rule_of_law, printing_press
- Core idea: Anyone who brings a new and useful device or process gets the sole right to make and sell it for a short fixed term (10 to 20 years), on condition that he files a description full enough for a skilled craftsman to copy it. This answers the inventor's dilemma: an invention costs time and money to perfect but can be copied at once, so without protection he either does not invent or keeps it secret and it dies with him. Minimum design: open to all, novelty test, fixed term, public register of descriptions, right to sell or license, and a court that stops copiers.
- Pitfalls:
  - Confusing patents with royal monopolies over existing trades (salt, soap, playing cards): those enrich favourites, raise prices and discredit the whole idea
  - Granting the right without a full written description: the public then gets nothing when the term ends
  - Terms that are too long or too broad block the next improvement (Watt's patent held back high-pressure steam until 1800)
  - Proposing free entry for inventors in a guild town: it attacks the guilds' right to control who practises a craft
  - Claiming patents caused the Industrial Revolution: historians disagree; most inventors of the time earned little from them
- History: greece: c. 500 BC – Sybaris is said to have given cooks a one-year monopoly on a new dish (anecdote in Athenaeus, citing Phylarchus); china: no pre-modern equivalent: techniques were kept in families or state workshops; 1898 first patent regulations, short-lived; east_asia: 1885 – Japan's Patent Monopoly Ordinance; europe: 1421 – Florence grants Brunelleschi a three-year monopoly for a cargo barge; 1474 Venetian statute (novelty, registration, 10 years); 1624 English Statute of Monopolies (14 years, true and first inventor); written specifications become the rule in England in the 18th c.; 1791 France; americas: 1790 – United States Patent Act
- Read:
  - Christine MacLeod, Inventing the Industrial Revolution: The English Patent System, 1660–1800 (1988)
  - Joel Mokyr, The Lever of Riches (1990)
